title: The Underground Railroad
text:
Before the American Civil War, thousands of enslaved people escaped from the South to the free states and Canada. Many were helped along the way by an informal network that came to be called the Underground Railroad. It had no headquarters and no membership list. It was made up of free Black communities, formerly enslaved people, Quakers and other white abolitionists, each of whom usually knew only the next few links in the chain. The secrecy protected everyone.

In Philadelphia, William Still, a free Black clerk with the Pennsylvania Anti-Slavery Society, helped run the city's Vigilance Committee, which sheltered, fed and moved fugitives onward. Against all caution, he kept written records of the people he helped, their names, where they came from and how they escaped, hiding the notes so they could one day reunite families. One of the people he interviewed turned out to be his own brother, whom his mother had been forced to leave behind in slavery decades earlier.

Still's records include Henry "Box" Brown, who had himself shipped from Richmond to Philadelphia in a wooden crate in 1849, and the many trips of Harriet Tubman, who returned south again and again to guide others out.

After the war, in 1872, Still published his notes as The Underground Rail Road, one of the few detailed records of how the network actually worked, told largely through the stories of the people who escaped.
lesson: A loose network of people who each do their part, and trust the next person, can achieve what no single hero could. Small, reliable links make a strong chain.
people: William Still, Harriet Tubman, Henry "Box" Brown, Vigilance Committee members
location: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, and routes across the eastern USA and Canada
source: William Still, The Underground Rail Road (1872); Eric Foner, Gateway to Freedom (2015)
